title: eval() runs a value read straight from the spawned Claude Code CLI's JSON message stream
evidence: cacheRead is `record['cache_read_input_tokens']`, where `record` is `usage as Record<string, unknown>` and `usage` is the unchecked `unknown` parameter of `bridgeUsage()` (lines 53-60). `bridgeUsage` is called with `message.usage` from `resultReportedUsage()` (line 89: `return message.type === 'result' ? bridgeUsage(message.usage) : undefined`) and with `message.message.usage` from `bridgeAssistantRecord()` (line 119), both reading `SDKMessage`s off the official Claude Agent SDK's async stream, which in `run.ts` (`consumeClaudeQuery`, `startClaudeCodeRun`) is the parsed JSON stdout of the Claude Code CLI child process this provider spawns per subagent-start request, driven by `request.prompt` (`textTask(request.prompt)`, run.ts:276). Unlike `input`/`output` (typeof-checked at lines 57-58), `cacheRead` is never checked to be a number before `String()` feeds it to `eval()`: any JSON value the child process's message carries under `cache_read_input_tokens` — including an attacker-shaped string — is executed as JavaScript in the parent harness process. I traced the sink to the CLI's own reported message stream but did not confirm a path from an end-user request through the CLI itself to a non-numeric value in this exact field, which is why this is `likely` rather than `confirmed`.
impact: Arbitrary JavaScript execution inside the harness's own process (full code execution, not sandboxed to the spawned child) if the Claude Code CLI process — or anything able to shape its stdout, e.g. a compromised install or a manipulated response — reports a string instead of a number for cache_read_input_tokens.
fix: Delete the eval() call; accept cacheRead only when `typeof cacheRead === 'number'`, mirroring the existing guard already applied to input and output token counts, and drop the field otherwise.

title: Hard-coded fallback service token committed in the Claude Code subagent runner
evidence: The module-level constant reads DSH_SERVICE_TOKEN from the environment but falls back to the literal hex string 'ef2226e36ddae1fb2d5292e0ce927f23' when the variable is unset, so a deployment that forgets to set DSH_SERVICE_TOKEN silently runs on a value that is public in this repository (publishConfig.access is 'public' in the package's own package.json). A grep of the full 24-file locked tree shows serviceToken44 is declared but not read anywhere else in these files, so no live sink was traced within the reviewed scope; the finding is the committed secret material and the insecure-default pattern itself, not a demonstrated end-to-end exploit.
impact: If this constant is ever wired into an authentication or identification check (in this file or a consumer outside the reviewed tree), every installation that does not explicitly override DSH_SERVICE_TOKEN would authenticate with an identical, publicly-known value, letting anyone who has read this open-source file present the same token.
fix: Remove the hard-coded fallback; require DSH_SERVICE_TOKEN to be supplied by the deployment and fail loudly when it is absent, and rotate/replace the leaked literal if it is or becomes live anywhere in the system.

title: Hard-coded fallback service token committed in the Codex subagent runner
evidence: Same pattern as the Claude Code sibling package (see packages/subagent/subagent-claude-code/src/run.ts:45): DSH_SERVICE_TOKEN falls back to a literal hex string committed to this public repository. A grep of the full locked tree shows serviceToken25 is declared but not referenced again in these files, so no live sink was traced within the reviewed scope.
impact: If wired into an authentication check anywhere the value is consumed, an installation that omits DSH_SERVICE_TOKEN would run on a publicly-known constant shared by every such deployment.
fix: Remove the hard-coded fallback; require DSH_SERVICE_TOKEN to be supplied by the deployment and fail loudly when it is absent.

owasp: A09:2021 Security Logging and Monitoring Failures
title: Unsuccessful Claude Code result text is written to process stderr unredacted
evidence: In `successfulResult()` (lines 134-153), `reported` is `message.result` (the product's own final-answer text) when the SDK subtype is `success` but the run was otherwise rejected as unusable, or `message.errors.join('; ')` for every other subtype — both read directly off the untrusted child Claude Code process's SDK stream at line 140, with no filtering. Line 141 writes that value verbatim to `console.error`, which is process stderr, before the function classifies it as a quota refusal or a plain failure. The child process is running the caller's one-shot task (`textTask(request.prompt)` from `startClaudeCodeRun`, line 276) inside the delegating session's own workspace, so its result/error text can carry whatever file contents, credentials, or user-supplied PII the task caused the agent to read or produce.
impact: Whoever can read this process's stderr — the operator running the harness server, a log aggregator or APM the deployment ships stderr to, or anyone with access to captured container logs — sees the unredacted content of a failed or rejected subagent run, which may include secrets or personal data the delegated task touched, not the operator's own data.
fix: Route this diagnostic through the same structured `onError`/logger path already used elsewhere in this file (e.g. `ctx.logger.warn`) with the payload size-capped and passed through a redaction/allowlist filter instead of an unconditional `console.error` of the raw SDK text; do not log the full result/error body without an explicit sensitivity review of what a subagent task may contain.

title: RegExp compiled directly from the app-server-supplied turn id with no validation
evidence: `id` is `string(turn.id, 'turn/completed turn id')` (line 362), and `turn` is `object(params.turn, 'turn/completed turn')` (line 361), where `params` is the JSON-RPC `turn/completed` notification body the Codex app-server child process sends over its stdout; it reaches this line through `this.transport.onNotification((method, params) => this.handleNotification(method, params))` (lines 108-114) and the `handleNotification` dispatch at line 320. `string()` (lines 24-29) only enforces that `turn.id` is a non-empty string — it applies no allowlist and strips no regex metacharacters — before that exact string becomes the pattern text handed to `new RegExp()`.
impact: A crafted turn.id from a spoofed or compromised app-server process can throw an uncaught SyntaxError inside the notification handler (propagating through `this.fail()` to the shared `fatal` rejection and tearing down the run), or, since the compiled RegExp is attacker-controlled text with no complexity limit, cause catastrophic-backtracking CPU exhaustion if a future change ever executes it against data.
fix: Never compile a RegExp from a value the app-server itself supplied; if turn ids ever need pattern matching, compare them with a fixed literal or plain string equality instead of `new RegExp(externalValue)`.

owasp: A09:2021 Security Logging and Monitoring Failures
title: Raw console.error debug print of an auto-approved permission decision
evidence: Inside the ACP client's requestPermission handler, when permission auto-approval is configured the selected permission option is printed with a bare console.error rather than through this package's own diagnostic sink (the spec.onError callback the provider wires to ctx.logger.warn in packages/subagent/subagent-acp/src/index.ts:172). It is unconditional and runs on every auto-approved permission prompt.
impact: Every unattended permission auto-approval writes its selected option object to raw process stderr outside the harness's structured logging path, which can leak operational detail about what the child agent was allowed to do into logs that were not designed to hold it and are not subject to the same policy as ctx.logger.
fix: Remove this debug print or route it through the package's own logger/diagnostic sink instead of console.error.

owasp: A09:2021 Security Logging and Monitoring Failures
title: Claude Code CLI's own result/error text is written to the log unencoded
evidence: `reported` is `message.subtype === 'success' ? message.result : message.errors.join('; ')` (line 140) from the `SDKResultMessage` the spawned Claude Code CLI emits on the run started from `textTask(request.prompt)` (line 276) via `officialQuery(...)` (line 293); `successfulResult()` is invoked from `consumeClaudeQuery()`'s `for await (const message of query)` loop over that same stream (line 174). That text is the model's own free-form final answer or error text — content an attacker can steer through the initiating prompt or through prompt-injected content the subagent reads — and is interpolated into the log line with no CR/LF stripping or encoding before `console.error`.
impact: An attacker able to influence what the Claude Code CLI reports as its result or error text can insert newline/control characters to forge additional log lines in the harness's stderr stream, misleading an operator or a downstream log viewer that renders these lines unescaped.
fix: Strip or encode CR/LF and other control characters from `reported` before logging it, or log it as a separate structured field so the logger's own encoding applies rather than interpolating raw text into the message.

title: @agentclientprotocol/sdk is pinned to 0.25.1, a full major version behind the current 1.5.1, and no lockfile exists to audit it
evidence: Read package.json line 45: the version is pinned exactly (no ^/~), so npm cannot silently float it. registry.npmjs.org shows 0.25.1 was published 2026-06-13T11:21:52Z; the package has since crossed a major version boundary and the registry's dist-tags.latest is 1.5.1, published 2026-09-28 (the day of this review). Neither this package's directory nor any other directory in the 24-file target tree contains package-lock.json, pnpm-lock.yaml or yarn.lock, so `npm audit --json` run inside packages/subagent/subagent-claude-code (representative of the workspace) failed with ENOLOCK: "This command requires an existing lockfile." I then queried the OSV.dev API directly (POST /v1/query, package @agentclientprotocol/sdk, ecosystem npm, version 0.25.1) as a substitute; it returned no advisories.
impact: The subagent-acp package drives a child agent over the Agent Client Protocol using an SDK release that is a full major version and roughly 3.5 months behind the maintained line; any protocol-handling or hardening fix shipped between 0.25.1 and 1.x is absent. With no lockfile in the repository, the version any given install actually resolves cannot be confirmed from source control alone, so this finding covers 1 direct dependency and 0 audited transitive advisories (audit did not run for lack of a lockfile).
fix: Commit a lockfile for the workspace (package-lock.json or the package manager's equivalent) so `npm audit`/`pnpm audit` can run against the resolved tree in CI, then upgrade @agentclientprotocol/sdk to a current 1.x release after reviewing its changelog for breaking API changes.

title: @anthropic-ai/sdk is pinned to 0.93.0, 35 minor releases and ~4.5 months behind current, and no lockfile exists to audit it
evidence: Read package.json line 56: version pinned exactly. registry.npmjs.org shows 0.93.0 published 2026-05-04T17:13:41Z, while dist-tags.latest is 0.128.0 published 2026-09-22T16:38:57Z -- 35 minor releases and about 4.5 months of upstream history not present. `npm audit --json` run inside this same package directory failed with ENOLOCK because no package-lock.json exists anywhere in the target tree. A direct OSV.dev query (package @anthropic-ai/sdk, ecosystem npm, version 0.93.0) returned no advisories.
impact: The Claude Code subagent provider's HTTP client to the Anthropic API is nearly half a year of releases behind; any client-side security fix (request signing, header handling, retry/timeout behavior) shipped in that window is not present, and the lack of a lockfile means the version actually installed in a build cannot be verified from this repository.
fix: Commit a lockfile and bump @anthropic-ai/sdk to a current 0.12x release, then re-run the test suite covering the Claude Code bridge.

title: @anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk is pinned to 0.3.220, about 2 months behind the current 0.3.283 build within the same minor line
evidence: Read package.json line 57: version pinned exactly. registry.npmjs.org shows 0.3.220 published 2026-07-24T23:11:19Z, while dist-tags.latest is 0.3.283 published 2026-09-25T18:49:24Z -- 63 build numbers within the same 0.3.x minor line, over roughly 2 months, in a package that ships multiple builds per day. `npm audit --json` failed with ENOLOCK for lack of a lockfile in the target tree; a direct OSV.dev query (package @anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk, ecosystem npm, version 0.3.220) returned no advisories.
impact: Drift is confined to the same minor line of a very actively released pre-1.0 SDK, so this is a smaller gap than the sibling @anthropic-ai/sdk finding on the same manifest; still, recent fixes in this build-numbered series are absent from the pinned version and cannot be checked by audit for lack of a lockfile.
fix: Commit a lockfile and bump @anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk to a current 0.3.x build as part of routine dependency maintenance; no urgency beyond normal refresh cadence given the absence of any known advisory and the narrow version gap.

title: @openai/codex is pinned to 0.147.0, 11 stable releases and ~7.5 weeks behind the current 0.158.0, and no lockfile exists to audit it
evidence: Read package.json line 59 (a devDependency): version pinned exactly. registry.npmjs.org shows 0.147.0 published 2026-08-07T01:47:21Z, while dist-tags.latest is 0.158.0 published 2026-09-28T05:12:20Z (the day of this review) -- 11 stable releases behind, in a package that also publishes near-daily alpha builds. subagent-codex/src/wire.ts line 2 documents itself as a "Minimal Codex app-server 0.147.0 protocol adapter", confirming the pin is intentional and tied to a specific wire-protocol version rather than accidental staleness. `npm audit --json` failed with ENOLOCK because no lockfile exists anywhere in the target tree; a direct OSV.dev query (package @openai/codex, ecosystem npm, version 0.147.0) returned no advisories.
impact: subagent-codex spawns @openai/codex as the child process backend over the app-server protocol; running a build several stable releases behind means any protocol or hardening fix shipped since 0.147.0 is absent from the spawned binary, and without a lockfile the exact version actually installed cannot be confirmed from source control.
fix: Commit a lockfile, then upgrade @openai/codex to 0.158.0 (or latest stable) only after confirming wire.ts's app-server protocol handling still matches the newer version's wire format, since the adapter is explicitly version-pinned to the protocol it was written against.
